input_text: Can you explain how to measure loudspeaker power with a shunt resistor if my oscilloscope ground is shared with the amplifier?
raw_output:
Good question — the shared-ground constraint is exactly what trips most people up here, because a naive shunt placement creates a ground loop or shorts the resistor through the scope.

## The core problem

Your scope's BNC shields are tied to mains earth (and to each other). Most amplifier outputs are referenced to the amplifier's chassis ground, which is also mains earth. If you put a shunt resistor in the "low side" return of the speaker and try to measure across it with one channel, the scope ground clip will short out the resistor — you'll read ~0 V across it and possibly blow something.

## Option 1: High-side shunt with two channels, math subtract

This is the cleanest approach for a single-ended amplifier.

Both probes share the amplifier ground — no ground loop, nothing shorted.

Voltage across shunt: V_shunt = Ch1 − Ch2 (use the scope's MATH function). Current through speaker: I = V_shunt / Rshunt. Voltage across speaker: V_speaker = Ch2. Instantaneous power: P(t) = V_speaker(t) × I(t). Average (real) power: time-average of P(t) over an integer number of cycles.

Caveats: Common-mode rejection is limited by how well-matched your two channels are. Use the same probe type, same attenuation, and run a quick "probe both to the same point" check — you should see ~0 on the math channel. Keep Rshunt small (0.1–1 Ω, non-inductive, adequately power-rated) so the subtraction isn't dominated by noise. Vertical sensitivity matters: if the speaker sees 20 V and the shunt drops 0.2 V, you're subtracting two large numbers to get a small one.

## Option 2: Low-side shunt (only if amp output is truly floating)

This works only if the amplifier's negative output is not bonded to chassis/earth — true for many bridged (BTL) class-D amps and for battery-powered amps, but not for typical single-ended hi-fi amps. Verify with a DMM (continuity from AMP(–) to chassis/earth) before trusting this. For a bridged amplifier, neither output terminal is at ground — both swing relative to chassis. You must use Option 1 (or a differential probe / isolation), never a direct low-side measurement.

## Option 3: Differential probe or current probe (best, if available)

A differential voltage probe across the shunt removes the shared-ground issue entirely and avoids the subtraction-noise problem. A Hall-effect or AC current probe clamped around the speaker lead measures current directly with full galvanic isolation. No shunt needed. If you do this regularly, one of these is worth the money.

## What NOT to do

Don't "lift" the scope's earth pin to break the loop. It's a real shock hazard and most modern scopes have the ground bonded internally to the chassis anyway. Don't isolate the amplifier with a cheater plug for the same reason. If you need isolation, use an isolation transformer rated for the amp, or better, an isolated/differential probe.

## Computing the actual power numbers

Once you have V(t) and I(t) aligned in time: Real (average) power: P_avg = (1/T) ∫ V(t)·I(t) dt — most scopes have a built-in MEAN of a math channel that does this. RMS values: V_rms, I_rms from the scope's measurement menu. Apparent power: S = V_rms · I_rms. Power factor: PF = P_avg / S — for a real loudspeaker this will be < 1 because the impedance is reactive and frequency-dependent.

For a clean measurement, drive the amp with a sine wave at a frequency where you know the speaker impedance (or use a dummy load resistor instead of the speaker if you just want to characterize the amplifier).

input_text: Can you expoain how to measure loduspeaker power with a shunt resistor if my oscilloscope ground is shared with the amplifier?
raw_output:
Good question — this is one of those situations where the "obvious" wiring will short out part of your amplifier or give you garbage readings. Here's how to think about it.

## The core problem

If your scope ground is tied to mains earth (almost all bench scopes are), and your amplifier's output ground is also tied to mains earth, then both probe grounds are already at the same potential. That's fine for single-ended amplifiers, but it becomes a trap when:

The amplifier is bridge-tied-load (BTL) — both speaker terminals are driven, neither is ground. Clipping a scope ground to either terminal shorts half the bridge to earth and usually destroys the amp. The amp is class-D — same risk, plus high-frequency switching content. You put the shunt on the high side (between amp output and speaker) — the scope ground clip would short the amp output to earth.

## Safe shunt placement for a single-ended amp

Put the shunt on the low side, in series between the speaker's "cold" terminal and amplifier ground. Voltage across the speaker: probe the amp's hot terminal with CH1 (tip to Amp+, ground clip to Amp GND). Current through the speaker: probe the junction between speaker and shunt with CH2 (tip there, ground clip to Amp GND). Both probe grounds go to the same node (amp ground = scope ground), so nothing is shorted.

## If the amp is BTL or you can't trust the ground

You have three options, in increasing order of "right way to do it": Differential probe across the shunt (and another across the speaker). This is the clean solution. Two channels in subtract mode (A−B math): put CH1 on one side of the shunt, CH2 on the other, both ground clips to scope ground. Use CH1−CH2 in math. Current probe (Hall-effect clamp). Galvanically isolated, no shunt needed, no ground concerns.

Do not "float the scope" by lifting its earth pin. It's dangerous (chassis becomes live), it injects a lot of noise via the Y-capacitors in the scope's PSU, and it's been the cause of more than a few destroyed scopes and shocked engineers.

## Sizing the shunt

Pick Rshunt so V_shunt at full power is roughly 100–500 mV peak — enough resolution on the scope, small enough to not affect the load meaningfully. For an 8 Ω speaker at, say, 10 W: I_rms ≈ 1.12 A, I_peak ≈ 1.58 A. A 0.1 Ω shunt gives ~158 mV peak — good. Power dissipated in the shunt is ~0.13 W, so a 0.5 W or 1 W non-inductive resistor is fine. Use a non-inductive type (metal film, bulk metal foil, or a proper 4-terminal current-sense resistor). Wirewound shunts add phase shift at audio frequencies and will skew your power reading. For accurate power into a real (reactive) speaker load, remember that V and I are not in phase — the scope's mean-of-product math handles this correctly, but a simple V_rms × I_rms calculation does not. Always use instantaneous V × I averaged over time.

## Quick sanity check

Drive the amp with a 1 kHz sine into a known resistive dummy load (e.g. an 8 Ω 100 W power resistor) before connecting a real speaker. Verify V_rms across the load matches what the amp should deliver, I_rms = V_rms / 8 Ω, math channel mean = V_rms² / 8 Ω. If those three agree, your wiring and math are correct, and you can swap in the speaker.

input_text: Can you explzin how to measure lourspeaker power with a suhnt resistkr if my oscilloscooe ground is sharwd with the amplifier?
raw_output:
Good question — and the shared-ground constraint is the whole crux of it. With a single-ended scope on a grounded amp, you can't just stick a shunt in series with the speaker and probe across it, because one end of the shunt won't be at ground and you'll short something out the moment you clip the probe ground.

Here's how to do it safely and get a real power number.

**1. Put the shunt on the ground side of the load**

Now the bottom of the shunt is at the common ground. You can probe the top of the shunt with CH1 (single-ended) and read the voltage across Rshunt directly — that's your current sense, I = V_ch1 / Rshunt.

Pick Rshunt small compared to the speaker impedance (e.g. 0.1–0.5 Ω for an 8 Ω load) and non-inductive (wirewound is bad; metal-film, bulk-foil, or a proper 4-terminal current-sense resistor is good). Make sure it can dissipate I²·R at your test level.

**2. Get the voltage across the speaker**

You can't directly probe across the speaker with one channel because neither end is at ground. Two clean options: Two channels, math mode. CH1 = top of shunt (the speaker's "low" side). CH2 = amp output (the speaker's "high" side). Then V_speaker = CH2 − CH1. Most scopes have a MATH A−B function. At low shunt values CH1 is small and V_speaker ≈ CH2, but doing the subtraction is more correct. Approximate. If Rshunt ≪ Z_speaker, just use CH2 (amp output to ground) as V_speaker with small error (~Rshunt/Zspeaker).

**3. Compute power**

Use a sine wave at the frequency of interest (1 kHz is standard for a quick number; sweep if you care about the response). Read RMS values from the scope's measurement menu, not peak. P_avg = V_speaker(RMS) × I(RMS) × cos φ. For a resistive dummy load, φ ≈ 0 and P = V·I = V²/R. For a real speaker the impedance is complex and reactive, so the cos φ term matters — the scope's built-in "Phase CH1–CH2" measurement gives you φ directly.

**4. Things that bite people**

Don't ground-probe the wrong node. If you accidentally clip a probe ground to the amp's hot output (e.g., a bridged/BTL amp where neither terminal is ground), you short the amp through the scope's safety ground. BTL amps in particular cannot be measured this way at all with a grounded scope — you need differential probes or an isolation transformer. Verify your amp is single-ended ground-referenced before trusting the topology above. Many car amps, class-D amps, and pro power amps are bridged. Use a dummy load first (a known power resistor of the right impedance) to sanity-check your numbers before driving an actual speaker, especially at higher levels. Watch the shunt's self-heating — its resistance drifts with temperature, which skews the current reading.

If your amp turns out to be bridged, the cleanest fix is a pair of differential/high-voltage differential probes, or a small isolation transformer between scope and mains so the scope ground floats — but floating the scope has its own safety caveats and I'd only recommend it if you're already comfortable with it.

## The core problem

If your scope's ground is bonded to the amp's ground (which it usually is, via the mains earth on both chassis), you cannot put a shunt resistor on the "high" side of the speaker and probe across it directly with a single-ended scope channel. One side of the shunt would be at the amp's hot output, and clipping the scope ground there would short the output to earth.

## Safe approaches

**1. Put the shunt in the ground-return leg**

Now one end of R_shunt sits at amp ground. Probe the other end with a single channel — that voltage, divided by R_shunt, gives you speaker current directly. This only works cleanly if the amp is single-ended (not a bridged/BTL amp, where neither output terminal is at ground).

**2. Use two channels in A–B (differential math) mode**

Leave the shunt wherever you want (e.g., in series on the hot side). Put CH1 on one end, CH2 on the other, both referenced to scope ground, and display CH1 − CH2. Limitations: Common-mode rejection is poor at high signal levels — you're subtracting two big numbers to get a small one. You still cannot let either probe ground touch the hot node.

**3. Use a true differential probe**

The clean solution. A differential probe lets you measure across the shunt anywhere in the circuit, regardless of where ground sits. For bridged amps this is essentially mandatory.

**4. Isolate the scope (NOT recommended)**

People sometimes "float" the scope by defeating its earth pin. Don't. It puts the whole chassis at whatever potential your probe ground clip touches, it's a shock hazard, and it wrecks the scope's noise performance. Isolate the amp with an isolation transformer if you must, never the scope.

Low value: 0.1–1 Ω, non-inductive (wirewound is often inductive — use metal-film, metal-foil, or a proper current-sense resistor). Power rating: I²R at your peak current with margin. For a 100 W / 8 Ω test, peak current ≈ 5 A, so a 1 Ω shunt dissipates up to 25 W peak — use ≥50 W or drop to 0.1 Ω. Keep leads short to minimize added inductance, which will distort the current waveform at HF.

Once you have V_speaker (across the load) and I_speaker (= V_shunt / R_shunt): Instantaneous power: p(t) = v(t) · i(t) — most scopes have a math channel for this. Average (real) power: mean of p(t) over an integer number of cycles. For a resistive dummy load and a sine, P = V_rms · I_rms. For most amplifier-power measurements, replace the speaker with a non-inductive dummy load (e.g., 8 Ω 250 W resistor bank).
